items.title: Android tablets are back, but are they for you?
items.raw_content: Android tablets have always been a bit of a touchy subject, but it’s abundantly clear that the form factor is making a comeback. But, as someone who’s a fan of the smaller sizes, are you actually using the gargantuan Android tablets that every company seems obsessed with? In other words – are you the customer for the Android tablets these brands are selling? 9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. items.title: Everyone wants an electric pickup truck. I want more electric 125cc motorcycles
items.raw_content: If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove. Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here. more…

items.title: Practical Deep Learning-Based Block Demapping for mmWave MIMO Systems
items.raw_content:
Authors: Syed Asrar ul haq, Jesus O. Lacruz, Joerg Widmer, Sumit J. Darak

Deep learning is expected to play a central role in 6G systems, by enabling data-driven physical layer designs that can adapt to practical wireless impairments. This is particularly important for millimetre-wave (mmWave) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which are strongly affected by residual channel distortions, interference, and hardware non-idealities that are difficult to capture with analytical models. In this paper, we propose a deep learning-based soft demapper that performs block-wise processing of received symbols instead of conventional symbol-wise detection. The demapper employs a one-dimensional convolutional neural network to learn temporal structure induced by practical propagation and hardware effects, while producing soft bit outputs compatible with soft-decision decoding stages. The proposed approach is trained and evaluated for a 4$\times$4 wideband mmWave MIMO system at 60~GHz, using an over-the-air dataset collected across multiple days and settings. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over a conventional soft-decision demapper, including up to a 2.6$\times$ reduction in bit error rate for 16QAM and up to a 17.6$\times$ reduction for 64QAM under real over-the-air mmWave MIMO conditions. The proposed demapper is further implemented on a Zynq RFSoC platform using a reconfigurable convolution engine and fixed-point arithmetic, achieving an approximately 34.3$\times$ speedup compared to a processor-based implementation, and demonstrating that learning-based demapping can be deployed efficiently on resource-constrained edge hardware.

items.title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
items.raw_content:
Authors: Zhengyang Cheng, He Zhu, Zeyu Guo, Zihan Liu, Anbang Wu et al.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms.
  In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.

items.title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
items.raw_content:
Authors: Sunghyeun Woo, Javier Conde, Pedro Reviriego

A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. Two studies with plans fixed before data collection, across 13 open models from 3B to 70B parameters, compare the next action and subsequent task completion, with exact deterministic reruns. A new user turn that retains the failed exchange avoids the severe stopping failure observed in Llama models when that exchange is removed. It is non-inferior to history rewriting in pooled synthetic comparisons, but is not best for every model. We implement this form as an opt-in recovery layer within a deterministic inference engine and evaluate it on public benchmarks and a coding agent. On ToolMaze, it raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models; Loud/Quiet, 24 multi-turn tasks with visible failures and silent corruption, scored by final-state agreement, shows no measurable gain. A client given the exact fault kind performs better still. The findings support delivery as a distinct factor in recovery, not an engine-exclusive solution or a universal retry policy.

items.title: CU-3D: A Scalable Legality-Aware RTL-to-GDS Flow for 3D-IC Physical Design
items.raw_content:
Authors: Mingjun Wang, Guanqi Li, Yihan Wen, Lancheng Zou, Mingjun Li et al.

Face-to-face (F2F) hybrid bonds shorten interdie connections, but data, clock, and power-grid (PG) connections must be realized together. CU-3D is a RTL-to-GDS physical design flow based on commercial EDA tools. It derives role-compatible hybrid-bond (HB) sites from a 17-metal ASAP7-based technology model, complete HB footprints, and constructed PG geometry. To coordinate partitioning with placement flexibility, Scaled refines an inherited 2D placement, whereas Fresh places the receiving die first and uses its pin locations and clock loads to guide placement of the other die. Data and clock HB assignments are jointly optimized while retaining alternative data sites and reserving capacity for subsequent PG assignment. The selected HB sites and stacks are preserved during 3D clock-tree synthesis, supply-aware cell insertion, and routing. Across eleven designs, including a 133-macro processor, the flow achieves zero backend DRC violations and passes signal-connectivity checks. Nine paired designs admit lower-footprint, lower-power implementations; four improve setup WNS. On JPEG, early joint planning gains 87 ps and mobility-aware partitioning gains 346 ps. Path analysis explains why cell-delay savings can outweigh net-delay increases.

items.title: PRISM: Preference-based Reward and Uncertainty-Integrated Synthesis Minimization for RTL PPA Optimization
items.raw_content:
Authors: Armin Abdollahi, Negin Ashrafi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram

This paper introduces a budget-aware, multi-objective framework (called PRISM) for RTL optimization that improves power, performance, and area (PPA) while sharply limiting expensive commercial synthesis tool calls. Starting from a synthesizable baseline and functional testbench, the method iterates through LLM-driven rewrite generation, fast compile/simulation equivalence filtering, low-cost proxy feature extraction, and selective commercial synthesis tool (Synopsys Design Compiler (DC)) evaluation. To prioritize which candidates deserve high-quality synthesis, we train a preference-based reward model using pairwise ranking supervision derived from commercial synthesis tool outcomes, and combine ensemble uncertainty with a diversity-aware acquisition rule to avoid early bias and redundant evaluations. A key advantage is that PRISM maintains a best-tradeoff set G of non-dominated designs throughout the run: G preserves the best solutions found so far, is fed back into generation and refinement, and enables consistent, cumulative improvements rather than repeatedly restarting from the baseline. Across RTLLM v2.0 modules, the approach consistently yields post-synthesis gains under fixed commercial synthesis tool call budgets, and ablations confirm that reward-guided selection and candidate dropping are central to sample-efficient progress. PRISM efficacy is evaluated across multiple technology nodes (7 nm, 15 nm, and 45 nm) using identical pipelines without retraining.

items.title: When Is High-Bandwidth Flash Cost-Effective for LLM Inference?
items.raw_content:
Authors: Zhiyu An, Yiping Li, Wan Du

Can high-bandwidth flash (HBF) make LLM inference cheaper than adding GPUs? By storing weights closer to the GPU than SSD, HBF may reduce the number of GPUs needed for model capacity. However, this integration is only justified if it meets service targets and its cost is recovered. We simulate this integration using public component data across nine dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, five workloads, two GPU platforms, and 1--100 GPUs. At fixed demand, HBF reduces the minimum GPU count to meet a service target in 98 of 468 comparisons; majority of them are paused and short sessions, 63 remain cost-effective at half a GPU price per HBF stack. For single short-chat users, HBF enables large MoEs, e.g. DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2, to meet a relaxed service target on one RTX~4090 GPU, where conventional serving fails. At fixed GPU count, HBF improves throughput in 48\% of matched comparisons below 16 GPUs and 13\% at larger counts. Even at 100 RTX~4090-scale GPUs, cascaded HBF raises offline throughput by 16.4--26.5$\times$ for three large MoEs. We found savings and throughput gains arise in different scenarios.

items.title: Compute Regeneration through Re-Productization: Reorganizing Retired Edge AI Silicon into a Delivered Multilingual Service Robot
items.raw_content:
Authors: Hongyu Luo, Sun Tie, John Wang

Useful edge hardware can lose product support while retaining substantial computation. We treat this as systems design: compute regeneration here means re-productization, retaining the compute module while redesigning the surrounding product organization. Our case is GEdgeBot, a multilingual service robot built around a retired 32 GB Jetson AGX Xavier. A source-grounded inventory shows the box alone supplies inference, while the combined system exposes five on-device AI services, a seven-language speech chain, three sensing domains, and one deterministic seven-byte control boundary. AI and orchestration stay on the Xavier; finite motor-pulse generation on an STM32F407. Audits cover the six-mode control state machine, readiness barriers and sound orientation. Historical single-prototype measurements report 1,782 MB GPU memory with YOLO, Whisper-small, and NLLB-200 resident, a direct-control p99 deviation rising from 0.24 to 49.93 ms under concurrent AI load, and six of six trigger-to-follow demonstrations at 4.35 s mean latency, with conversational voice unavailable. A November campaign restores an isolated inference stack, re-measures AI workloads, and repeats control-frame runs. Driving two execution organisations with the same 6,000 measured 50 ms frame intervals shows the finite-pulse boundary removes host jitter from the pulse train but not the command start phase; its stopping bound is host-enforced, while the MCU 16-bit pulse field is unclamped. A six-check static audit exposes a host--MCU queue mismatch, and a 14-scenario replay executes the audited main() dispatcher across six modes with zero physical device opens and 54 contract-checked frames. Results support an existence claim and a reproducible architectural hypothesis, not fleet-level reliability. The 208 direct-control ratio remains unreplicated; MCU waveform capture and on-site fault injection remain open.

items.title: Priority-Aware Deficit Round Robin for AXI4 Bandwidth Fairness in ASAP-7nm Process
items.raw_content:
Authors: Tasmin Khan, Tishna Sabrina, Ch. Md. Rakin Haider

Modern systems-on-chip place real-time clients, processor cores and bulk data engines on the same AXI4 interconnect, where they contend for shared slaves. AXI4 fixes the ordering rules and carries a 4-bit quality of service (QoS) field, but leaves the service policy to the implementer, and that policy determines how long each master waits and how much bandwidth it receives once a slave saturates. We propose a QoS-aware deficit round robin (DRR) architecture that charges each grant in beats, and benchmark it against two architectures built behind the same port list: round robin, and QoS priority with anti-starvation aging. Charging in beats recovers bandwidth fairness while leaving every burst whole, so the address phase is issued once and locality for memory access is preserved. All three are driven by the same deterministic traffic generator and taken from RTL to GDSII on the ASAP7 7-nm predictive PDK. Under a 1:16 burst-length mismatch, the round robin and QoS architectures both hold the beat ratio between the two competing masters at 1:16, while our design brings it to 1:1 at full load. Mean read latency for the priority master falls from 95 cycles under round robin to 67 with QoS and 37 with QoS-aware DRR. At 500 MHz this serves the priority master in 74 ns against 190 ns. The measurements give a per-policy price and a traffic-based guide for choosing among the three.

items.title: ICLayout-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Custom Circuit Layout Design
items.raw_content:
Authors: Zhangmai Li, Tianrui Ma, Zheng Weng, Mo Zou, Zidong Du et al.

Large language model (LLM) agents are being explored for circuit design, but their ability to produce high-quality custom layouts has not been extensively evaluated. ICLayout-Bench is a benchmark in which agents use electronic design automation (EDA) tools to construct and optimize GDSII layouts from transistor-level circuit netlists. These layouts are evaluated using physical verification, parasitic extraction, and post-layout simulation. Layouts that pass the physical and functional checks are scored on electrical performance and area. The benchmark includes 165 tasks across 13 process design kits (PDKs), covering technology nodes from 3 nm to 180 nm. The tasks span analog, mixed-signal, and digital circuits in open-source and commercial EDA flows. The experiments evaluate 22 configurations spanning seven models on 21 public and 19 private tasks. Mean layout scores range from 4.22 to 80.26 on public tasks and from 1.43 to 67.01 on private tasks, on a 100-point scale. Higher reasoning effort does not consistently improve mean scores, and configurations with comparable scores can incur substantially different model costs.

items.title: A Per-Step Load-Balancing Engine for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
items.raw_content:
Authors: Jingyuan Li, Maolin Wang, Hayden So

In expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts serving, a layer finishes only when the most loaded GPU of its group does. Token routing shifts at every decode step and concentrates on a few experts, so most of the group's reserved GPU time waits on stragglers. Recovering that time means re-deciding, at every layer of every decode step, how each replicated expert's tokens divide between its copies. The exact linear-program solvers that make this decision optimally take longer than many of the layers they serve, and their working set outgrows GPU shared memory at deployment scale. We introduce Relief, a bidirectional pairwise relaxation that makes the linear program unnecessary, coming within a fraction of a point of the per-step optimum in a few passes of integer halving over the token counts. We build and measure three deployments, CUDA kernels on the serving GPU, the same verified engine on an FPGA over PCIe, and a fixed-function block beside the accelerator. On decode routing from three open MoE families, Relief holds the balance near the per-step optimum at every group size and layer time measured. Scored as effective utilization relative to that optimum, the kernel alone matches or exceeds every deployable scheme at every group size, from the hundred-microsecond layer on. The on-die engine widens that lead at every point, recovering up to 37.3 percentage points over the deployed static placement, while adding 0.02% of a current accelerator's transistors.
